EYEBROW: COCOM bench · PX1105R, NEO-M8T, ZED-F9P and mosaic-G5 · 2026-09-30 to 10-02
LEDE: How four GNSS receivers keep tracking through a rocket boost, and how much that depends on signal strength. Two simulated flights, a space shot (the traveler) and a short, hard burn (the hotshot), were played into the PX1105R, the u-blox NEO-M8T, the u-blox ZED-F9P and the Septentrio mosaic-G5 on the COCOM bench at signal levels from 9 dB under to 12 dB over the file's own, and each receiver was followed satellite by satellite through the burn. The mosaic-G5 also flew two flights to just over 80 km, which show where its export limit lies: at 600 m/s, with no altitude in it.

blocks.p: The traveler is modelled on Traveler IV's space shot. The hotshot is built for receivers that withhold their measurements above 515 m/s: it packs 10–30 g of boost into the 2.8 s before that speed, so the steepest satellite's Doppler rate sweeps from about 470 to 1400 Hz/s while they still report.

All four receivers saw the same files. The NEO-M8T's, the ZED-F9P's and the mosaic-G5's RF paths have 10 dB more attenuation than the PX1105R's. The mosaic-G5 also flew gentle_alt and spaceshot, the rig's August flights to 82.5 km, rebuilt in the same format at +6 dB (in its part).

0 dB is the file's own level (SignalSim at 45 dB-Hz). +6 and +12 dB are the same scenario regenerated at 51 and 57 dB-Hz; −3, −6 and −9 dB were made by adding calibrated noise as the file streamed. On the bench every satellite has the same level; under the sky the high satellites, which take the steepest Doppler rates in a boost, are the strong ones. Each receiver reads the levels its own way, so each part sets them against that receiver's own readings on the roof antenna (there are none for the ZED-F9P).

Each line is one satellite's line-of-sight Doppler rate through the burn: the rocket's acceleration along the line to that satellite, in Hz/s at the carrier. 51.5 Hz/s is 1 g straight at the satellite, so the high satellites draw the steepest lines. The marks show where the receiver lost a satellite and which ones it kept; each chart's caption gives the details.

notes: Files. One SignalSim file per flight and level, carrying GPS L1 C/A, Galileo E1 and BeiDou B1I together at 18.48 Msps centred on 1568.286 MHz, dated 2026-08-18. The HackRF's carrier runs about 23 Hz off its code at this frequency; uncorrected, GPS pseudoranges slide off the code and channels break every minute or so. Every file was corrected by −23 Hz, in the file or by the transmitter as it streamed.

Lower levels. SignalSim writes its noise into the file, so turning the transmitter down would not lower C/N0. The transmitter instead adds white Gaussian noise to every sample as it streams and scales the sum back to the file's own RMS: the transmit level and noise density stay put and every signal drops by the chosen amount. Checked offline on the file: asked 3, 6, 9 dB, measured 3.00, 6.00, 9.00; residual flat across the band; with no noise asked the output is byte-identical.

Higher levels. The same scenarios regenerated by SignalSim at 51 and 57 dB-Hz and carrier-corrected by the transmitter as it read them (it matches the offline correction tool to one count of rounding in 30 of 67 million bytes).
Transmitter. A buffered transmitter keeps 2 GiB of the file in memory ahead of the HackRF, so disk reads never hold it up.

Underruns. At 37 MB/s the HackRF's own buffer holds well under a millisecond, and it runs dry whenever USB delivery stalls; the host side never fell short. Each underrun shifts the signal late by the gap and drops every channel for 10–90 s. Across the USB cables tried the rate stayed at about 0.2–0.7 per minute (one cable was clearly worse); keeping the computer awake or the reader polling did not change it. Flying the mosaic-G5 on 10-02 it ran at about one a minute, as on the F9P sweep.

Re-flights. A flight whose boost an underrun could have touched (one between T−60 and T+30) was discarded and flown again: by hand on 09-30, automatically once from 10-01. Each part lists its discarded flights.

blocks.lede: PX1105R in navigation mode 9 (speed-lag reduced), cold restart on the pad, elevation mask 3°, no C/N0 mask. Lock comes from its 1 Hz channel status (a channel counts as locked while its C/N0 stays within 6 dB of its pad level) and delivered measurements from its 20 Hz raw messages; loss times are good to ±0.5 s.

blocks.p: Pad C/N0 as the receiver read it in each run, against the same PX1105R on the roof antenna (2 h log, 09-29, elevation ≥ 10°): median GPS 39, BeiDou 41, Galileo 40 dB-Hz; above 60° GPS 42, BeiDou 47, Galileo 41. A 20-minute log that day read 1 dB lower for GPS and BeiDou and 6 dB lower for Galileo. The readout compresses at the top (+12 dB in the file reads as +8 to +9), so the sky's median sits at about the 0 dB run and its high satellites between the 0 and +6 dB runs.

findings: GPS has a threshold between 38 and 44 dB-Hz. At 38 dB-Hz and below, 12 of 13 GPS satellites lose lock at 110–245 Hz/s (2–5 g along the line of sight) and stay lost. At 44 they drop in the steep first 1–3 s but are locked again within a second or two, while the fix is still running, and 9 of 13 are locked at burnout at up to about 740 Hz/s. At 47 dB-Hz, 11 of 12 never let go.

BeiDou B1I is the most robust. All 7 held at 39 dB-Hz, at up to 820 Hz/s, and 6 of 9 at 37 (two of its three losses came at 590–600 Hz/s), but only 1 of 7 at 34, where they went at 130–240 Hz/s in the first 2.5 s.
Galileo E1 is the weakest in the boost at every level. Even at 44 dB-Hz, 4 of 6 lost lock at 300–370 Hz/s. Below about 41 dB-Hz on the pad the receiver barely acquires it in this wide file.

The receiver withholds measurements it is still tracking. While its own fix runs, the raw stream drops satellites whose channels are locked at full C/N0, and releases them when the fix stops at the 515 m/s limit (T+6.2 to 6.5). Anything built on the raw stream sees those satellites as lost.

Lose too many in the boost and it goes blind for minutes. At 34 dB-Hz it kept 1 GPS and 1 BeiDou, cut its active channels from 41 to 2–12, stopped searching, and output nothing until 4 BeiDou were locked again at T+256; GPS came back only with the fix, at T+282. At 31 dB-Hz it lost everything and reacquired near apogee (T+140), when the rocket was slow.

notes: Underruns in these runs (each dropped every channel for 10–25 s): 0 dB none; −3 dB about T+227 and T+260 (it blanked the re-entry, so the fix came back at T+285.7); −6 dB about T+136 (above 80 km); −9 dB none; +6 dB about T+337 and T+347 (fix ends T+346); +12 dB about T−74 and T+62. None touched a boost. They became more frequent after the PortaPack was power-cycled (none in the 0 dB run before it, 1–3 per run after).
Discarded flights. The first −3 dB (the PortaPack dropped off USB at T+31), and two −3 dB and one +6 dB attempt whose underruns at T−59 to T−23 blanked the boost.

blocks.p: The speed passes 515 m/s at T+2.8 and stays above it until T+22.2, so the receiver's fix covers only the first 2.8 s of the burn.

findings: Most GPS is lost in the first 2.5 s, even at 47 dB-Hz. The hotshot starts at 10 g, so line-of-sight rates reach 300–600 Hz/s within half a second. At 47 dB-Hz, 8 of 13 GPS satellites lost lock by T+2.4, at 460–650 Hz/s, and 5 were locked at burnout, at up to 500 Hz/s. At 44 dB-Hz 4 were locked at burnout, all four after an early loss; at 39, none. The traveler reached rates like these only 5–7 s into its burn.

BeiDou holds through 40 g. All 6 BeiDou satellites were locked at burnout at 50 and 46 dB-Hz, and 5 of 6 at 40, through line-of-sight rates of up to 1340–1620 Hz/s. The receiver kept delivering their pseudoranges while its fix was suspended: 7–9 m RMS in the burn above 515 m/s and 4–5 m in the coast that follows, against about 1 m on the pad.
Galileo is lost at every level, all of it by T+2.4, at 200–590 Hz/s.

At 34 dB-Hz it loses everything in the first 1.5 s (GPS and BeiDou at 120–580 Hz/s); the fix stops at T+0.85 and nothing comes back before the file ends at T+120. In the traveler at this level it stayed silent until T+256.

Fix. It stops at T+2.5–2.9, at the 515 m/s limit, and is back at T+22.3 as the speed falls under 515 m/s again, at +12, +6 and 0 dB. When the fix stopped, its own speed was 25–49 m/s behind the truth.

blocks.h3: Error against Doppler rate, all ten runs

blocks.p: Every delivered measurement through the burn, split at the first 515 m/s crossing. While its fix runs, the PX1105R withholds many locked satellites, and what it does deliver is good: none of 711 in the hotshot and 47 of 3780 in the traveler were more than 10 m off (those 47 all from low GPS satellites, 9–16° elevation, at 90–130 Hz/s, up to 15 m). Once its fix stops it releases everything, and through the rest of the burn a fifth to a quarter of that is wrong: 62 of 240 in the hotshot and 724 of 3348 in the traveler, GPS worst (up to 1.7 km off, many of them slow satellites, so not only the dynamics), Galileo up to 444 m, BeiDou up to 28 m.

blocks.lede: u-blox NEO-M8T tracking GPS, Galileo and BeiDou: raw measurements (RXM-RAWX) and navigation (NAV-PVT) at 10 Hz, satellite status at 1 Hz, airborne <4 g dynamic model, 460800 baud. Above 515 m/s it withholds all raw measurements, not only its fix, so its tracking can be followed only to the first 515 m/s crossing (T+2.8 on the hotshot, T+6.3 on the traveler). A satellite counts as lost if its valid pseudoranges stop for 0.5 s or more before that point.

blocks.p: Pad C/N0 as the M8T read it in each run, against the same receiver on the roof antenna (09-29, elevation ≥ 10°): median GPS 41, Galileo 36 dB-Hz; above 60° GPS 46 and Galileo 42 (only three readings). That log had no BeiDou. With 10 dB more attenuation in front of it, the M8T reads the bench files 2–4 dB lower than the PX1105R from +12 to 0 dB, while on the sky it reads GPS 2–4 dB higher. So for the M8T the sky's median sits at about the +6 dB run and its high satellites at about +12 dB, some 6 dB higher on the bench scale than for the PX1105R. Its readout also flattens at the bottom: GPS 34 dB-Hz at −6 dB against 35 at 0 dB on both flights, though 6 dB of noise was added (BeiDou did drop 5 dB).

findings: It keeps reporting almost every satellite to its cut-off. At T+2.8, when it stops, it still flagged valid pseudoranges from GPS 10 of 13 at +12 and +6 dB and 10 of 10 at 0 and −6 dB; Galileo 8/8, 8/8, 5/6 and 2/2; BeiDou all, at every level.

But its fastest satellites go wrong. Below about 400 Hz/s every valid-flagged measurement was within 6 m, on both flights and at every level. Faster than that, the highest satellites drift off while still flagged valid: Galileo first passed 10 m at 495–853 Hz/s and GPS at 666–840 Hz/s, and they kept going, to 100–550 m by 1000–1400 Hz/s, with Doppler errors of 13–250 m/s. Its tracking fell far behind the motion without letting go. In the hotshot's first 2.9 s, 297 of its 2570 valid-flagged measurements were more than 10 m off. BeiDou, all below 21° elevation here (under 550 Hz/s), stayed within 2.5 m.

That explains its odd GPS drops. At +12 and +6 dB it dropped its three highest GPS satellites (40–66° elevation, T+1.1 to 2.6) once their errors had reached 8–47 m; at 0 and −6 dB it kept reporting the same three while they ran 160–405 m off. Its high Galileo satellites stayed in the output however far off they were, except E26 at 0 dB, dropped at T+2.5 after running 340 m off.

Fix. Its own speed kept up with the truth to the end: 3, 3, 7 and 23 m/s behind at the last fix (T+2.7–2.8, +12 to −6 dB). The fix was back at T+22.3–22.4 at every level and the raw measurements at T+22.4–22.5, as the speed fell under 515 m/s at T+22.2.

figure.name: m8t_hot_boost.png
figure.alt: NEO-M8T hotshot boost chart: each satellite's line-of-sight Doppler rate up to the raw cut-off, one panel per signal level
figure.caption: Per satellite: solid while the M8T delivered valid pseudoranges, with a magenta band wherever those were more than 10 m off the truth (◆ where that starts); × where one stopped for 0.5 s or more, △ still flagged valid when it withheld everything; grey beyond that, where it reports nothing. The panel titles count the satellites that went over 10 m.

findings: Every satellite to the cut-off, at every level. At T+6.3 it still had GPS 13/13, 9/9, 13/13 and 11/11 (+12 to −6 dB), Galileo 7/7, 7/7, 5/5 and 2/2, and BeiDou 5/5, 5/5, 4/4 and 5/5. The traveler's rates by then reach only about 570 Hz/s.

And at these rates its measurements are good. Through the burn to its cut-off every satellite stayed within 0.1–3.6 m RMS, Doppler within 0.8 m/s, at every level, except at −6 dB, where Galileo E13 (55°) passed 10 m at 422 Hz/s and ran up to 181 m off before it dropped at T+6.0: 18 of the traveler's 5433 valid-flagged measurements, the only ones over 10 m. Above 80 km and in the descent, wherever no underrun intervened, 95 % of its errors were within 0.4–1.8 m for GPS and BeiDou and 0.6–5 m for Galileo (the +6 dB run's descent, after an underrun at T+297, reads several times worse).

Raw follows the speed; the fix waits for the descent. Raw measurements stop whenever the speed is over 515 m/s (T+6.3 to T+98, and T+206 to T+282 coming down) and flow in between, though the rocket is above 80 km then. The fix stays off from T+6.1–6.2 until T+282.0–282.2, the same at every level; at the last fix its speed was 1 m/s behind the truth. At +6 dB a 3 s burst of raw from 5 GPS satellites came at T+87, while the speed was still over 515 m/s.

blocks.p: Every valid-flagged measurement from ignition to the raw cut-off, on one rate axis for both flights. The errors stay within a few metres until the line-of-sight Doppler rate passes about 400–500 Hz/s, then the fastest satellites peel away. The traveler stops reporting at 515 m/s before its rates pass about 580 Hz/s, so only one weak Galileo satellite gets there; the hotshot reaches 1400 Hz/s first.

notes: How the errors were worked out. As for the PX1105R: the truth is SignalSim's own trajectory, the receiver clock is solved from all satellites each epoch, and each system's constant offset is taken out on the pad. The M8T logged no navigation data, so its satellites' orbits come from the PX1105R captures of the same scenarios, which carry the same broadcast data. Errors are taken at the M8T's own time tags, as for the PX1105R (its clock runs about 3 ms ahead of GPS time, but correcting for that fitted the burn worse); its Doppler fits the truth 0.01 s earlier (the PX1105R's, 0.03 s).

Discarded flights. The −6 dB traveler took three flights: the first had underruns from T+0.8, the second was stopped partway through (operator error), the third was clean (underruns only at T−168 and at the end of the file). Every other M8T flight was clean from T−60 to T+30 first time.
Underruns outside the boost window show in some run plots as short gaps or clock steps (hotshot +12 and −6 dB, traveler +12 and +6 dB); none touched a boost.

blocks.lede: u-blox ZED-F9P (ArduSimple board, firmware HPG 1.13) tracking GPS, Galileo and BeiDou on its own USB port: raw measurements (RXM-RAWX) and navigation (NAV-PVT) at 10 Hz, satellite status at 1 Hz, airborne <4 g dynamic model. Like the M8T it withholds all raw measurements above 515 m/s, so its tracking can be followed only to the first 515 m/s crossing (T+2.9–3.0 on the hotshot, T+6.3 on the traveler); a satellite counts as lost as for the M8T. Its RF path has the same 10 dB of extra attenuation as the M8T's.

blocks.p: There is no roof log for the ZED-F9P to set its levels against. On the bench it reads the files within 1 dB of the PX1105R at every level (GPS 47, 44, 39 and 33 dB-Hz from +12 to −6 dB), and 2–5 dB above the M8T from +12 to 0 dB, behind the same attenuation as the M8T. At −6 dB it tracked no Galileo satellite at ignition on either flight (the M8T had two).

findings: It keeps most satellites to its cut-off, but lets go of more than the M8T. At T+2.9 (T+3.0 at −6 dB), when it stops, it still flagged valid pseudoranges from GPS 11 of 13 at +12 and +6 dB, 10 of 13 at 0 dB and 9 of 10 at −6 dB; Galileo 4/8, 4/8 and 5/8 (none at −6 dB); BeiDou 7/8, 6/8, 6/8 and 3/3. Its two highest Galileo satellites, E13 (55°) and E26 (68°), went at T+1.1 at +12 and +6 dB (E13 also at 0 dB) while still within 9 m.

Its fastest satellites go wrong too, but it drops most of them within tens of metres. Below 500 Hz/s every valid-flagged measurement was within 3.2 m, on both flights and at every level. Faster than that a few high satellites drift off while still flagged valid: GPS first passed 10 m at 596–883 Hz/s, Galileo at 628–679 and BeiDou (C35 and C36, 41–48°) at 695–920 Hz/s. At +12 and +6 dB every one was dropped within 11–53 m; at 0 dB two BeiDou reached 82 and 188 m (C36 dropped at 13 m, then reappeared that far off in the last two epochs) and Galileo E21 was still 14 m off at the cut-off; at −6 dB three GPS satellites ran 214–400 m off, two of them still flagged valid at the cut-off (and BeiDou C35, picked up 3 s before ignition, 355 m). In the hotshot's first 2.9 s, 104 of its 2616 valid-flagged measurements were more than 10 m off, against the M8T's 297 of 2570.

Fix. Its own speed kept up with the truth to the end: 1–2 m/s behind at the last fix (T+2.8) from +12 to 0 dB, 29 m/s at −6 dB (T+2.9). The fix was back at T+22.3 and the raw measurements at T+22.4 at every level, as the speed fell under 515 m/s at T+22.2.

figure.name: f9p_hot_boost.png
figure.alt: ZED-F9P hotshot boost chart: each satellite's line-of-sight Doppler rate up to the raw cut-off, one panel per signal level
figure.caption: Drawn like the M8T's chart: solid while the F9P delivered valid pseudoranges, with a magenta band wherever those were more than 10 m off the truth (◆ where that starts); × where one stopped for 0.5 s or more, △ still flagged valid when it withheld everything; grey beyond that. The panel titles count the satellites that went over 10 m.

findings: Nearly every satellite to the cut-off, at every level. At T+6.3 it still had GPS 13/13, 13/13, 9/9 and 11/11 (+12 to −6 dB), Galileo 9/9, 9/9 and 6/7 (none tracked at −6 dB), and BeiDou 8/8, 8/8, 7/7 and 5/5.

And its measurements are good. Through the burn to its cut-off GPS and BeiDou stayed within 0.4–1.9 m RMS and 0.25 m/s in Doppler at every level, Galileo too at +12 and +6 dB. The exception is Galileo E26 (68°) at 0 dB: it passed 10 m at 462 Hz/s (T+4.0) and ran to 90 m before it dropped at T+5.1, 11 of the traveler's 6210 valid-flagged measurements and the only ones over 10 m. Above 80 km, 95 % of its errors were within 0.8–1.7 m.

A fix above 80 km, sometimes. Raw measurements stop whenever the speed is over 515 m/s (T+6.3 to T+98, and T+206 to T+282 coming down) and flow in between, as on the M8T. But at +12, +6 and 0 dB its fix came back with them at T+98.0, 88 km up, and followed the rocket through apogee at 102.2 km until T+206 (T+197 at 0 dB, where an underrun cut it): the only fix any of the three receivers gave between the two crossings. At −6 dB it computed one position at T+98 (86.6 km), flagged it invalid and gave nothing more until T+282.0. In August, on a slower climb through 80 km with its fix running, the same receiver held its fix off from 80.1 to 82.2 km. So above 80 km its fix is a bonus, not something to count on. Otherwise its fix stopped at T+6.2 (1 m/s behind the truth) and came back at T+282.0, at every level.

notes: How the errors were worked out. As for the M8T: the truth is SignalSim's own trajectory, the receiver clock is solved from all satellites each epoch, each system's constant offset is taken out on the pad, and the orbits come from the PX1105R captures of the same scenarios (the F9P logged its own navigation data; shared orbits keep the three receivers comparable). Errors are taken at the F9P's own time tags. Its Doppler fits the truth with no delay (the M8T's 0.01 s, the PX1105R's 0.03 s late). Its pseudoranges fit the truth best about 11 ms after their time tags (the M8T's about 5 ms); left in, as for the others, that adds a few metres that grow with speed, about 6 m by 515 m/s on the traveler.

Its other ports. The F9P's first eight flights were discarded. The board had kept its saved settings on the ports nothing reads: UART1 at 38400 baud and I2C sending the full NMEA set every epoch, which at 10 Hz with 25–30 satellites backed up its transmit buffers (UART1 peaked at 104 %). Its large raw messages then stopped about 45 s after each cold start (10–45 % of the pad's epochs arrived at +12 and +6 dB) while every small fix message came through. With UART1, UART2, I2C and SPI output turned off before each flight (RAM only), 96–100 % arrived.

Discarded flights (second sweep). Hotshot +12 dB: a 1.6 ms underrun at T−110, outside the boost window, made the receiver step its clock by the same 1.6 ms, and a GPS channel that never followed the step stayed 469 km off into the burn. Hotshot +6 and −6 dB and traveler +6 and 0 dB were each flown once more after an underrun in the boost window, and hotshot 0 dB twice more (underruns at T−3 and T−16). Traveler +12 and −6 dB were clean first time.

Underruns outside the boost window show in some run plots: the hotshot −6 dB run's gap at T+85–95 (underrun at T+81), the traveler 0 dB run's lost fix at T+197 and missing BeiDou and Galileo until T+282 (T+195), and the traveler −6 dB run's descent (T+323–337). Each file also ends in one.

blocks.lede: Septentrio mosaic-G5 P3 (firmware 1.0.0) on its own USB port: raw measurements (SBF MeasEpoch), their noise and multipath estimates (MeasExtra) and its position (PVTGeodetic) at 20 Hz, receiver dynamics set to its most dynamic (setReceiverDynamics, High, Unlimited: the high-dynamics level and unconstrained motion), cold-started before every flight. Unlike the others it withholds its fix and raw measurements above 600 m/s, not 515, so its tracking can be followed to T+3.1 on the hotshot and T+7.0 on the traveler; a satellite counts as lost as for the M8T (a gap of 0.5 s or more in valid pseudoranges), measurements are read at 10 Hz like the u-blox parts' and only on the files' signals. Its RF path is the F9P's, with the same 10 dB of extra attenuation. It also flew the rig's two 82 km flights, rebuilt in the same format.

blocks.p: On the roof antenna (2 h log, 10-02, elevation ≥ 10°) the mosaic-G5 reads median GPS 42, BeiDou 41 and Galileo 44 dB-Hz, and above 60° GPS 46, BeiDou 49 and Galileo 46: the highest of the parts logged there (the PX1105R read GPS 39 and 42, the M8T 41 and 46). On the bench it reads the files within 1 dB of the ZED-F9P and the PX1105R (GPS 47, 44, 39 and 34 dB-Hz from +12 to −6 dB). So for the mosaic the sky's GPS median sits between its 0 and +6 dB runs and its high satellites between +6 and +12 dB, and BeiDou's high satellites at about +12 dB. At −6 dB it acquired no Galileo and almost no BeiDou in the 180 s pad after its cold start.

findings: It keeps everything to 600 m/s at +6 dB, and its measurements stay right. At T+3.1, when it stops, it still flagged valid pseudoranges from GPS 13/13 at +6 and 0 dB, Galileo 9/9 at +12 and +6 dB and BeiDou 9/9, 9/9 and 6/6 from +12 to 0 dB, at line-of-sight Doppler rates up to 1470 Hz/s. None of its 992 valid-flagged measurements at +6 dB was more than 10 m off the truth (the largest 2.6 m), nor any of the 794 that can be judged at +12 dB (0.9 m). At 0 dB it lost three of its four Galileo satellites, E26 (68°) at 574 Hz/s, E27 and E29 at 378 and 476 Hz/s, and E29 went 14 m off before it went: 1 of 658 measurements over 10 m.

+12 dB: the rig's clock step, not the burn. It dropped six GPS satellites in the first second, at 125–525 Hz/s: exactly the six a transmitter underrun on the pad (a 2.6 ms gap at T−55) had left 790.9 km off. It did the same on the traveler at +12 dB. Both +12 dB flights had such an underrun; their errors over 100 km are the rig's and are left out (see the notes).

−6 dB: it cannot hold a 10 g ignition. With GPS alone at 34 dB-Hz it lost 12 of 13 satellites in the first 1.7 s, at 160–740 Hz/s, and its last fix, at T+1.15, still gave 1.8 m/s against a true 137 m/s. It picked the satellites up again at T+13.6, already at 636 m/s, and stayed blocked until the speed fell under 597 m/s at T+16.05. With no fix it did not know its speed, so one low satellite's measurements came out past 600 m/s, to T+4.0.

Fix. Its own speed kept up with the truth to the limit: 585.1–586.3 m/s at the last fix (T+3.04), within 0.2 m/s of the truth, and blocked from the next epoch at 599.9–601.9 m/s. It was back at T+16.04, at 596.7–596.8 m/s, from +12 to 0 dB, with its raw measurements.

figure.name: mos_hot_boost.png
figure.alt: mosaic-G5 hotshot boost chart: each satellite's line-of-sight Doppler rate up to the 600 m/s cut-off, one panel per signal level
figure.caption: Drawn like the u-blox charts, to the mosaic's own cut-off at 600 m/s (T+3.1): solid while it delivered valid pseudoranges, with a magenta band wherever those were more than 10 m off the truth (◆ where that starts); × where one stopped for 0.5 s or more, △ still delivered when it withheld everything. +12 dB: the six GPS × are the satellites a pad underrun left on the old clock. −6 dB: GPS only, and no truth comparison (the clock solution needs Galileo or BeiDou).

findings: Everything to 600 m/s, down to 0 dB. At T+7.0 it still had GPS 13/13 at +6 and 0 dB, Galileo 9/9 at +12 and +6 dB and 8/9 at 0 dB, and BeiDou 9/9 at every level down to 0 dB. Through the burn all its measurements were within 1.8 m at +12 and +6 dB (none of 2063 and 2201 over 10 m); at 0 dB Galileo E26 (68°) went 21 m off at 276 Hz/s before it was lost at T+1.2, 3 of 2151 measurements. At +12 dB it lost the four GPS satellites a pad underrun had left 806 km off, and nothing else.

−6 dB: GPS alone, and it goes wrong before it goes. It held 5 of 13 GPS satellites to the cut-off. Six of the eight it lost drifted 11–107 m off while still flagged valid, at 111–266 Hz/s: 24 of its 460 measurements were over 10 m, the most of any mosaic run.

A fix above 80 km, on every flight. Its fix stopped at T+6.95, at 596.5–598.5 m/s by its own speed, came back at T+89.5 as the speed fell under 595 m/s, 83.6 km up, and followed the rocket through apogee at 102.2 km until the descent passed 600 m/s at T+215.2 (83.3 km); it was back at T+279.0, at 594 m/s and 31.9 km. The same at every level, −6 dB included. Between the crossings the ZED-F9P also gave a fix at +12 to 0 dB; the PX1105R and the M8T did not.

The coast tells transmitter gaps from tracking. Every flight but the −6 dB one had an underrun in the coast; after each the mosaic tracked again within seconds but would not mix channels on the old and new clock, and gave no fix (error 6, too few measurements after outlier rejection) for 8–70 s. With no underrun (−6 dB) its fix ran unbroken from T+89.5 to T+215.1.

blocks.h3: The export limit: 600 m/s, and no altitude

blocks.p: The mosaic-G5 withholds its fix whenever its own speed passes 600 m/s, PVTGeodetic reporting position output prohibited due to export laws, and lets it go a few m/s lower. Its raw measurements stop and start with the fix, to the epoch. Altitude plays no part: it gave a fix all the way through apogee on three flights that climb past 80 km. 600 m/s is the speed in the current EU and US dual-use rule for airborne GNSS receivers, which has no altitude term; the other three parts stop at 515 m/s and, except sometimes the F9P, at 80 km.

Two of the four flights here are the rig's August flights to just over 80 km, rebuilt in the sweep's wide format at +6 dB with a 180 s pad: gentle_alt climbs at 3 g to 997 m/s and 82.5 km; spaceshot burns 12 s at about 15 g to 1341 m/s and the same apogee. On the 3 g climb its speed passes 600 m/s by 1.5 m/s per epoch, which pins the edge: its last fix read 599.3 m/s by its own speed, and it was blocked one epoch, 1.5 m/s, later. Coming down, each flight crossed 600 m/s again at 63–83 km, where the speed changes slowly: its last fixes read 599.9–600.0 m/s, and the next epoch, 600.2–600.6 m/s true, was blocked. On gentle_alt its fix ran through both 80 km crossings without a break; the ZED-F9P, on the same climb in August, held its fix off from 80.1 to 82.2 km.

It lets go 2–10 m/s under the limit, latest in the hard deceleration of re-entry (590 m/s on gentle_alt), which looks more like a margin on its own estimate than a fixed second threshold. Above 80 km it gave 2347 fixes on the traveler (to 102.2 km), 914 on gentle_alt (every epoch of its 46 s up there) and 704 on spaceshot, where an underrun just past 80 km cost 10 s.

blocks.h3: Error against Doppler rate, all eight runs

blocks.p: Every valid-flagged measurement from ignition to the 600 m/s cut-off, as for the u-blox parts. From +12 to 0 dB they stay within about 3 m to the end, past 1400 Hz/s in the hotshot; the only ones over 10 m are Galileo E29 and E26 at 0 dB. At −6 dB, GPS alone, they go wrong from about 110 Hz/s.

runs.caption: speed and altitude (truth and the receiver's own; amber where over 600 m/s), vertical acceleration, valid raw pseudoranges per satellite (magenta where more than 10 m off the truth, T−5 to T+30), satellites per epoch and fix, and pseudorange and Doppler errors on axes that are linear near zero and logarithmic beyond (dashed: ±10 m); boost close-up on the right.

notes: How the errors were found. As for the u-blox parts (m8t_accuracy.py: the pooled broadcast ephemeris, the SignalSim truth, the receiver clock solved from Galileo and BeiDou), on the mosaic's MeasEpoch read at 10 Hz on GPS L1 C/A, Galileo E1 and BeiDou B1I, with no Doppler delay. Elevations come from the same ephemeris and the true position: after a cold start on the rig the mosaic reports them only for satellites in its almanac, GPS and a few Galileo.

Clock steps. An underrun delays the signal by the gap, 1–3 ms and once 210 ms. The mosaic steps its clock to follow, but a channel that misses the step stays that far off: 790.9 km for the 2.638 ms gap on the +12 dB hotshot, a whole multiple of the gap times the speed of light. No tracking error comes near that, so errors over 100 km are counted as the rig's and left out; on the clean flights all of them come after an underrun late in the flight.

Underruns. About one a minute on 10-02, the rate the F9P sweep saw. Each one dropped every mosaic channel for 10–20 s, or about 60 s at −6 dB, and on the pad it sometimes raised a false export block, 0.5–7 s at rest, before its velocity settled. One −6 dB traveler (not shown) took an underrun at T+70 while already blocked and stayed blocked to the end of the file, through apogee and down to 16 km at 92 m/s; its re-flight, with no underrun at all, released normally.

Flights kept. Each level was flown once more after an underrun between T−60 and T+30; the flight shown is the cleaner of the two. Hotshot: +12 dB the first (the second had a 210 ms underrun burst at T−32), 0 dB the second (one underrun at T−17, recovered by ignition), −6 dB the second. Traveler: +12 dB the first (the second had an underrun at T−11 and too few satellites at ignition), 0 dB the second, −6 dB the third, flown to check the blocked flight.

Setup. Firmware 1.0.0 has no position or velocity covariance output, and no setting for its signal-authentication check: about 36 s into every pad it flagged that its signals may not be authentic (it may be connected to a simulator), which on this firmware only raises the flag. Galileo navigation-message authentication (OSNMA) was off. Nothing was saved to the receiver; the runner set it up after each cold start.

findings: The mosaic-G5 keeps the most satellites, and the right measurements, up to its limit at 600 m/s. Through the hotshot at +6 dB it still delivered every satellite at T+3.1 (GPS 13/13, Galileo 9/9, BeiDou 9/9), at line-of-sight Doppler rates up to 1470 Hz/s, and through the traveler every one at +6 dB and all but one Galileo at 0 dB. From +12 to 0 dB, 4 of its 8859 valid-flagged measurements in the two burns were more than 10 m off the truth, the largest 21 m: against 297 of 2570 for the M8T and 104 of 2616 for the F9P in the hotshot's first 2.9 s alone. Its weakness is the bottom: at −6 dB it had only GPS on the pad, lost nearly all of it at the hotshot's 10 g ignition, and in the traveler 24 of its 460 measurements went over 10 m.

Its export limit is 600 m/s, with no altitude in it. It withholds its fix and raw measurements together whenever its own speed passes 600 m/s (pinned to 1 m/s on the 3 g climb of gentle_alt and on the re-entries) and lets go 2–10 m/s lower. Below that it kept its fix through apogee on all three flights that pass 80 km, 102.2 km on the traveler, with no break at 80 km either way. The other three parts withhold at 515 m/s, and the PX1105R and M8T above 80 km as well.

Below 515 m/s the two u-blox receivers keep more satellites than the PX1105R, but some of their valid-flagged measurements are wrong. At the last moment all three can be compared the M8T and the F9P still reported most satellites, where the PX1105R had lost most GPS and all Galileo in the hotshot and most GPS at 0 dB and below in the traveler. Counting only measurements within 10 m of the truth, they still keep more: in the hotshot GPS 10/13 (M8T) and 11/13 (F9P) against the PX1105R's 5/13 at +12 dB, and 7/10 and 10/13 against 0/13 at 0 dB, Galileo 4–5 of 8 against none; in the traveler all or all but one (GPS 13/13 and 9/9 against 1/13 at 0 dB). But above about 500 Hz/s their fastest satellites drift off without losing their valid flag, where none of the 711 measurements the PX1105R delivered in the hotshot before 515 m/s was more than 10 m off. The M8T keeps reporting them tens to hundreds of metres off; the F9P drops most of them within tens of metres, except at −6 dB (in the hotshot 297 of the M8T's 2570 valid-flagged measurements were over 10 m, 104 of the F9P's 2616). The levels did not favour the u-blox parts: the M8T read the files 2–4 dB lower than the PX1105R, the F9P the same.

Above 515 m/s only the PX1105R and the mosaic-G5 deliver measurements, and above 600 m/s only the PX1105R, many of them wrong. The M8T and the F9P withhold their raw measurements along with their fix (on the traveler, T+6.3 to T+98 and T+206 to T+282), the mosaic-G5 above 600 m/s (T+7.0 to T+89.5 and T+215.2 to T+279.0). The PX1105R keeps tracking and releases its measurements once its fix stops; at the sky's levels its BeiDou held through both burns (to about 820 Hz/s in the traveler and 1600 Hz/s in the hotshot). But between 515 m/s and burnout, 62 of the 240 measurements it released in the hotshot and 724 of 3348 in the traveler were more than 10 m off: GPS worst (up to 1.7 km), Galileo up to 444 m, BeiDou up to 28 m. In the coast that follows most settle back to a few metres.

No receiver's raw output can be used unscreened in a boost. The M8T and the F9P go wrong at high Doppler rates while they are still reporting, below 515 m/s. The PX1105R's habit of withholding measurements while its fix runs screens its output until then, but what it releases afterwards needs the same checking. The mosaic-G5 came closest, but its −6 dB measurements went wrong too. A navigation filter using any of them through a boost has to test each measurement before it trusts it.

Between the 515 m/s crossings only the F9P, sometimes, and the mosaic-G5, always, gave a fix. On the traveler the PX1105R's and M8T's fixes stopped at T+6.1–6.5 and came back at T+282.0–282.4, within half a second of the speed falling under 515 m/s, at every level where they still tracked (except the PX1105R's −3 dB run, after an underrun); in between, the speed is over 515 m/s or the rocket is above 80 km. The F9P's did the same at −6 dB, but at +12, +6 and 0 dB it also gave a fix from T+98 to T+197–206, 88 km up and through apogee, as soon as the speed fell under 515 m/s; in August, on a slower climb, it held its fix off above 80 km. On the hotshot all three were back at T+22.3–22.4, within 0.2 s of the crossing. The mosaic-G5's fix came back at T+89.5 on the traveler, as the speed fell under 595 m/s at 83.6 km, and ran through apogee to T+215.2 at every level; on the hotshot it was back at T+16.0, under 597 m/s.

Lose too much in the burn and the PX1105R goes blind. At 34 dB-Hz it lost nearly every satellite in the boost and then stopped searching: on the hotshot it had no fix again before the file ended at T+120; on the traveler it output nothing until T+256 (its fix still came back at T+282). The M8T, the F9P and the mosaic-G5 were back on time at −6 dB on both flights (the mosaic once stayed blocked to the end of the file, after a transmitter underrun hit it mid-block; its re-flight was normal).

Signal level matters far more to the PX1105R. Its GPS needs about 44 dB-Hz to ride through the traveler (the threshold lies between 38 and 44), and even 47 dB-Hz was not enough in the hotshot; its BeiDou holds down to about 37–40 dB-Hz and collapses at 34. The M8T's and F9P's satellite counts barely moved with level. What level did change is how far their fast satellites went wrong before they were dropped: at +12 and +6 dB the M8T dropped three GPS satellites once they had gone wrong, which at 0 and −6 dB it went on reporting 160–405 m off; the F9P dropped its own within 11–53 m at +12 and +6 dB, but at −6 dB reported three GPS satellites as far as 214–400 m off.

What a real flight should look like. On the roof the PX1105R reads GPS 42 and BeiDou 47 dB-Hz above 60° elevation, where a boost's steepest rates fall: between its 0 and +6 dB runs. Expect it to hold BeiDou through either burn, GPS partly through the traveler and little of it through a hotshot-like burn, and to lose Galileo. The M8T reads GPS 46 above 60° on the roof, about its +12 dB run: expect it to report nearly everything until 515 m/s, accurately in a traveler-like burn but with its fastest GPS and Galileo satellites going wrong (and some dropped) in a hotshot-like one, and then nothing until the rocket slows. There is no roof reading for the F9P, which reads the bench files like the PX1105R: expect it to behave like the M8T until 515 m/s, dropping rather than keeping most of its fastest satellites as they go wrong, then nothing until the rocket slows, perhaps with a fix near apogee. The mosaic-G5 reads GPS 46 and BeiDou 49 dB-Hz above 60° on the roof, between its +6 and +12 dB runs: expect it to keep all three systems, with accurate measurements, through either burn until 600 m/s, then nothing until the speed falls under about 595 m/s, and then a fix whatever the altitude, apogee included.

Limits of the bench. Every satellite shares one level, unlike the sky. The wide file costs Galileo about 2 dB on the PX1105R and slows its acquisition. The M8T's and F9P's cut-offs hide the hotshot's last 1.0–1.2 s of burn (30 to 40 g), the mosaic-G5's its last 0.9 s. Transmitter underruns, from the USB link, forced re-flights whenever one hit a boost; on the F9P one before the boost window spoiled a flight too, by leaving a channel on the old clock, so its runs were checked for that. The mosaic-G5 suffered most from underruns: each dropped all its channels, and for up to a minute afterwards it would not give a fix from channels left on the old clock.
